prompt: The Secret's `data` holds the key as `dGVzdA==`. What does that encoding protect the key from?

choices.text: Nothing: `base64 -d` turns it back into the key
choices.why: Base64 is an encoding with no secret in it. The capture decoded it with one command, and anybody who can read the Secret does the same.

choices.text: From anybody who lacks the cluster's encryption key
choices.why: That describes encryption at rest, which protects the disks. The value in the Secret is readable by everybody Kubernetes lets read it.

choices.text: From being read by pods in other namespaces of the cluster
choices.why: Namespaces and RBAC decide who reads a Secret, and they do it whatever the value looks like. The encoding adds nothing to that.

choices.text: From being used after the Secret is deleted
choices.why: Deleting the Secret deletes one copy. The key stays valid in IAM, and every other copy of it keeps working.

prompt: To avoid a key, a team adds `s3:GetObject` to the EKS node role, so the resizer can read the bucket. What did they actually grant?

choices.text: Read access to the resizer pods, and to the kubelet that starts them
choices.why: The kubelet does use the node role, but so does every other process on the machine that asks the metadata service.

choices.text: Nothing, because a node role is limited to ECR and the CNI
choices.why: A node role holds whatever policies are attached to it; there is no such limit, which is exactly the danger.

choices.text: Read access to the pods whose service account names the node role
choices.why: Service accounts name roles in IRSA, through an annotation. The node role reaches pods through the metadata service instead, with no annotation.

choices.text: Read access for any pod on those nodes
choices.why: The node role is handed out by instance metadata, so it is granted to the machine and to whatever runs on it, not to one workload.

prompt: In the capture, `get-session-token` answered with an `Expiration`. How many hours after the request does that temporary credential stop working?
hint: Compare the time in `Expiration` with the time `create-access-key` printed a second earlier.

prompt: Where does a key placed in `secret.yaml` end up? Choose every place the section names.

choices.text: In the repository, and in every clone of it, if the file was committed
choices.why: Git keeps every committed version, so deleting the file later leaves the key in history and in every clone.

choices.text: In every pod that mounts the Secret
choices.why: Mounting is the purpose of the Secret: each such pod holds the key in its environment.

choices.text: In a CI log that printed the environment
choices.why: One of the accidental copies the section lists, and among the hardest to find afterwards.

choices.text: In STS, which keeps a copy so it can expire the key
choices.why: STS issues temporary credentials and keeps no copy of an IAM user's key; nothing expires the key at all.

choices.text: In the node's instance metadata service
choices.why: The metadata service hands out the node role's temporary credentials. It knows nothing of a key kept in a Secret.

prompt: What does `aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider --url "$ISSUER" --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com` add to the account?

choices.text: A role that every pod of the cluster is able to assume
choices.why: A provider grants nothing by itself. Which tokens become which role is decided by a role's trust policy.

choices.text: An IAM user for the cluster, with a key the pods share
choices.why: IRSA creates no user and no key. The pod calls STS itself with its token.

choices.text: The issuer's private key, so that IAM signs every token the pods present
choices.why: Kubernetes signs the tokens and keeps the private key; IAM is told where to fetch the public keys that check them.

choices.text: A record that tokens signed by this issuer and audience are trusted
choices.why: That is the whole of it: IAM learns whose signatures to accept, and a trust policy can then name the provider.

prompt: A role's trust policy names the cluster's provider and the `aud` condition, but somebody deleted the `sub` line. Which pods are able to assume the role now?

choices.text: None of them, because the policy is now invalid and IAM rejects it
choices.why: A statement with fewer conditions is still valid IAM. It is wider, not broken, which is why the mistake goes unnoticed.

choices.text: Only the pods in the namespace whose service account created the role
choices.why: Roles are not created from a namespace, and nothing in the policy names one any more.

choices.text: Every pod in the cluster with a token for `sts.amazonaws.com`
choices.why: Every pod's token comes from the same issuer, so without `sub` the policy no longer tells one service account from another.

choices.text: Pods of other clusters in the same account
choices.why: Another cluster has another issuer and another provider, and the `Federated` principal still names this one.

prompt: Complete the action an IRSA trust policy allows, the call that trades a Kubernetes token for credentials: `"Action": "sts:___"`
hint: It names what the caller brings: an identity from the web.

prompt: To save editing, a team writes the trust condition as `StringLike` with `system:serviceaccount:shop:*`. A year later a colleague adds a service account `shop:export` for an unrelated job. What follows?

choices.text: `shop:export` is refused until somebody adds it to the role
choices.why: That is what `StringEquals` with one name would do. The wildcard was written precisely so nobody has to add anything.

choices.text: The role stops working, since two service accounts now match
choices.why: A condition matching several subjects is valid; each token is tested on its own.

choices.text: Nothing changes unless `shop:export` runs on the same node
choices.why: Nodes play no part in IRSA's trust decision. It is the token's subject that is tested.

choices.text: `shop:export` is able to assume the role the day it is annotated with it
choices.why: The wildcard matches every service account in the namespace, including ones that did not exist when the policy was written.

prompt: The role, the provider and the trust policy are right. The annotation was added to service account `photos` an hour ago, and the resizer pod, running since yesterday, still gets `AccessDenied` from S3. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The OIDC provider needs a thumbprint before IAM will trust it
choices.why: The API reference says the thumbprint is optional, and an EKS issuer's certificate is checked against AWS's trusted authorities.

choices.text: The pod predates the annotation, so it never got the token
choices.why: The role is wired into a pod when the pod is created. Restarting the deployment creates pods that have it.

choices.text: IRSA takes a day to reach a new service account
choices.why: There is no such delay in IRSA. The token is written as the pod starts.

choices.text: S3 refuses temporary credentials that came from a web identity
choices.why: S3 accepts them like any other signed request; they are ordinary STS credentials.

prompt: Put the IRSA exchange in the order it happens on AWS, from the pod's first AWS call.
items: The SDK reads AWS_ROLE_ARN and the token file
The SDK sends the token to STS's AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
STS fetches the issuer's public keys
STS checks the signature and the trust policy's conditions
STS returns credentials for one hour
The SDK signs the S3 call with them
trap: Checking the conditions before fetching the keys: STS cannot trust a single claim until the signature over all of them is verified.

prompt: With `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` exported but the test keys still set, `aws sts get-caller-identity` answers as moto's user. Why?

choices.text: moto refuses to do the exchange while the test keys are still present
choices.why: moto never sees an exchange in that case: the command line does not attempt one.

choices.text: The SDK looks for keys in the environment before it looks for a token
choices.why: The credential chain stops at the first source that answers, and environment keys come first. A real pod has none.

choices.text: The token file must be in `/var/run/secrets`
choices.why: Any path works; the variable says where it is, and the capture used `~/aws/token`.

choices.text: `AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME` was missing
choices.why: It is optional. Without it the SDK invents a session name and still does the exchange.

prompt: moto gave credentials for the token `not-a-token` and for a role that does not exist. What does the exchange run on the laptop actually establish?

choices.text: That the SDK side works: two variables make it do the exchange
choices.why: That is the part moto really exercised, the same code path a pod runs. The verification is the part it skipped.

choices.text: That the trust policy in `trust.json` is correct for the photos pod
choices.why: moto never opened it. A wrong `sub` would have produced the same answer, which is why the policy has to be checked on AWS.

choices.text: That STS accepts an unsigned token as long as it is short
choices.why: STS refuses an unsigned token of any length with `InvalidIdentityToken`; moto reads none.

choices.text: That roles are created on demand by STS
choices.why: IAM creates roles. moto simply does not check that the ARN names one.

prompt: On AWS, match each token STS is handed with what STS answers.

pairs.left: A token whose signature does not check against the issuer's keys
A correctly signed token past its exp
A correctly signed token for system:serviceaccount:shop:default
A correctly signed token for system:serviceaccount:shop:photos

prompt: The denial ran with `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT=5`: bucket, photo, role, permission, exchange. You want to repeat it with the IAM OIDC provider created too, inside the unchecked window, before the exchange. What count do you start moto with?
hint: Count one per AWS request the command line sends. Writing a file sends none.

prompt: With EKS Pod Identity, what links the service account `shop:photos` to its role?

choices.text: An annotation on the service account
choices.why: That is IRSA's link. Pod Identity has nothing to annotate in Kubernetes.

choices.text: A `sub` condition in the role's trust policy
choices.why: Pod Identity's trust policy names the service `pods.eks.amazonaws.com` and no service account at all.

choices.text: An association in EKS
choices.why: An association names the cluster, the namespace, the service account and the role, and replaces both the annotation and the provider.

choices.text: An IAM OIDC provider per namespace
choices.why: Pod Identity needs no OIDC provider at all, per namespace or per cluster.

prompt: A cluster runs some workloads on managed node groups and others on a Fargate profile. Which can use EKS Pod Identity?

choices.text: Both, as long as the add-on is installed
choices.why: The add-on is a DaemonSet, and a DaemonSet has no node to run on under Fargate.

choices.text: The Fargate pods only, since AWS runs their agent
choices.why: AWS runs no Pod Identity Agent for Fargate pods; that is why they are excluded.

choices.text: Neither, until the cluster is recreated
choices.why: Pod Identity is added to an existing cluster by installing the add-on and creating associations.

choices.text: Only those on EC2 nodes; the rest keep IRSA
choices.why: The agent runs on nodes you have, and Fargate gives you none, so lesson 12's Fargate pods use IRSA.

prompt: In the laptop run, what did the command line send to the stand-in agent at `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI`?

choices.text: A GET with the token as `Authorization`
choices.why: That is the container credentials protocol: the token from `AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE`, sent as a header, and JSON credentials back.

choices.text: A signed `AssumeRole` request using the test keys
choices.why: The keys had been unset; the command line had nothing to sign with, which is why it asked the agent.

choices.text: The role ARN, so the agent knows which role to assume
choices.why: The pod does not choose its role here. The association decides it, and the stand-in had the role written in.

choices.text: A PUT for an IMDSv2 token, as on an EC2 instance
choices.why: That is the metadata service's protocol from lesson 7. The agent is a different endpoint with a different protocol.

prompt: Ten teams share one cluster, a namespace each, and each must read only `s3://shop-data/<its namespace>/`. Which approach keeps it to one role?

choices.text: IRSA, with ten `sub` conditions in one trust policy
choices.why: That lets ten service accounts assume the same role, and then each of them reads every prefix the role allows.

choices.text: The node role, with one statement per prefix in its permission policy
choices.why: The node role is shared by every pod on the node, so it cannot tell the teams apart at all.

choices.text: Pod Identity, matching the prefix to the session's namespace tag
choices.why: Every session carries its namespace as a tag, so one permission policy can say "your own prefix" for all ten.

choices.text: One IAM user per namespace, its key in a Secret
choices.why: Ten users, ten keys that never expire, and still no single role: the section's first wrong answer, ten times.

prompt: Match each workload with the way this course would give it AWS credentials.

pairs.left: A pod on an EKS Fargate profile
A pod on EC2 nodes, in eight clusters that are replaced at every upgrade
A cron job on a plain EC2 instance

right_distractors: an IAM user's key in a Secret

prompt: IRSA and Pod Identity are both set up correctly, and an audit still finds a pod reading a bucket with the node role's credentials. What setting from lesson 7 closes that path?

choices.text: A shorter `DurationSeconds` on the pod's role
choices.why: The pod's role is not the one being used; the node role is, through the metadata service.

choices.text: A `sub` condition on the node role's trust policy
choices.why: The node role trusts the EC2 service, and the metadata service hands it to any process that asks; `sub` belongs to web identity tokens.

choices.text: IMDSv2 required, with a hop limit of 1
choices.why: The token's answer cannot make the extra hop into the container, so the pod never reaches the node's credentials.

choices.text: Deleting the pod's service account
choices.why: The pod would lose its own role and keep the node's, which is the opposite of the fix.

prompt: Every CloudTrail event from the resizer shows the session name `botocore-session-1792166400`, and twenty replicas look identical. What would have made the events say which workload it was?

choices.text: Giving each replica its own IAM user and key
choices.why: That brings back the static key and its whole cost, to solve a naming problem.

choices.text: Setting `AWS_ROLE_SESSION_NAME` in the pod
choices.why: Without it the SDK invents a timestamped name; with it the session says which workload, as `photos-pod` did in the capture.

choices.text: Adding a thumbprint to the OIDC provider
choices.why: A thumbprint concerns the TLS of the issuer's key endpoint and says nothing about sessions.

choices.text: Raising the projected token's lifetime above a day
choices.why: A longer token changes how often the kubelet rewrites it, not what the session is called.

prompt: Which of these does the pod identity webhook add to a pod whose service account carries the IRSA annotation? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `AWS_ROLE_ARN`
choices.why: The role from the annotation, which the SDK puts in its exchange.

choices.text: `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`
choices.why: The path of the projected token, the other half of what switches the SDK to the exchange.

choices.text: A projected volume holding a token for `sts.amazonaws.com`
choices.why: The token itself, valid for a day and rewritten by the kubelet before it runs out.

choices.text: `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`
choices.why: No key goes into the pod at all; avoiding exactly that is what IRSA is for.

choices.text: `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI`
choices.why: That variable is Pod Identity's, pointing the SDK at the agent; IRSA does not set it.

prompt: `aws eks create-pod-identity-association` answered moto's `404 Not Found` page. What does that tell you about AWS?

choices.text: That the cluster `shop` was not found
choices.why: A missing cluster is a JSON `ResourceNotFoundException` from EKS, not an HTML page.

choices.text: That the role needs `sts:TagSession` first
choices.why: The role already had it in `pod-trust.json`, and a policy problem is never answered with a 404 page.

choices.text: Nothing: moto 5.2.3 has no route for the call, and on AWS it returns the association
choices.why: The 404 is moto's web framework. The behaviour on AWS has to be read in AWS's documentation, as the section did.

choices.text: That Pod Identity is not offered in sa-east-1
choices.why: Nothing in the answer names a region; it is the emulator that lacks the call.

prompt: A team moves the resizer from IRSA to Pod Identity. Which change does the resizer's own code need?

choices.text: A call to the EKS Auth API before the first S3 request
choices.why: The agent makes that call. The application only sees the SDK find credentials.

choices.text: Reading the token file and passing it to S3
choices.why: S3 never sees a Kubernetes token in either mechanism; it sees requests signed with STS credentials.

choices.text: None, given a recent enough SDK
choices.why: Both mechanisms are found by the SDK's credential chain, so the code is the same; an old SDK is the one thing to check.

choices.text: Replacing `AWS_ROLE_ARN` with the association's id
choices.why: The association's id is never given to the pod; EKS sets the two container variables instead.
